result.summary: Adds an Events IPC interface over Cap'n Proto that provides a single, ordered, pull-based stream of block and mempool notifications. External clients can subscribe to block connections and disconnections, as well as mempool additions and removals, with optional serialized payloads and configurable byte-bounded buffering. It also updates internal mempool tracking to report the mempool sequence number when transactions are removed due to being mined in a block.
result.problem: Existing ZMQ notification mechanisms have significant gaps for external applications: block notifications skip intermediate blocks during rapid updates or IBD, transaction notifications do not distinguish mempool acceptance from transactions included in blocks, and sequence notifications omit payload data and block-inclusion removal reasons. Furthermore, ZMQ buffer limits count messages rather than total bytes, risking unbounded memory consumption when full blocks are queued.
evidence: Cites long-standing user pain points regarding inability to distinguish mempool entry from block inclusion in PR #19462, PR #23624, and PR #7753 ("pain point of https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/19462#issuecomment-658304417, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/23624#issue-1065790580 and https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/7753")
result.scope_notes: Because libmultiprocess currently lacks native mapping from std::variant to Cap'n Proto unions, the PR manually implements union conversions in events-types.h.
result.card: Bitcoin Core PR #36985 adds an Events IPC interface that streams block and mempool events in a single ordered, byte-bounded stream. It addresses persistent gaps in ZMQ notifications, which skip intermediate blocks, cannot differentiate between mempool admissions and block transactions, and cannot stream ordered payloads alongside sequence updates. The author cites unresolved ZMQ pain points from PRs #19462, #23624, and #7753. The change also modifies mempool removal tracking so that removals caused by block inclusion retain their sequence numbers.

risk.why: A flaw in notification queuing, synchronization in KernelNotifications, or mempool removal accounting could cause memory exhaustion or thread deadlocks during block connection.
